newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian space station collides with cargo craft.
newsitem.headline: Russian space station collides with cargo craft.

text.p: Russia's Mir space station collided on Wednesday with a cargo craft during a manual docking exercise, raising fresh doubts about the safety of the poorly financed Russian space programme.

Russian space officials described the collision as "the most serious accident in recent times" involving the ageing vessel but said there was no immediate danger to a U.S. astronaut and two Russian cosmonauts on board.
But they admitted that the three-man crew, U.S. Michael Foale and Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin, faced power problems.

"The cosmonauts say there is a fall in the electrical supply...and as a result of the collision a hole (in the scientific module used for the docking) has developed whose size is still unclear," said mission control head Vladimir Lobachyov.

"This was the most serious accident in recent times," he told a news briefing at the mission control centre near Moscow. He said it was not yet clear what had caused the accident but added that a technical malfunction might have been at fault.
The unmanned, Russian-owned Progress cargo craft collided at 1.20 p.m. (0920 GMT) with the Spektr scientific module attached to the main section of Mir, causing a partial loss of air pressure.
A spokesman for the U.S. space agency NASA said earlier on Wednesday that the crew had been able to seal off the damaged compartment after the collision.
The main part of the 11-year-old station was not affected by the collision but a solar battery on the Spektr may have been damaged, a Russian spokeswoman told Reuters by telephone.
A space expert who requested anonymity said damage to the solar battery could cause serious problems but declined to give details until the full picture emerged.
NASA officials said the Mir crew could leave at any time in a three-seat Russian Soyuz spacecraft but added that the evacuation of the station was not planned.

Despite the comparative safety of Foale, the chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives Science Committee urged NASA on Wednesday to begin a safety review of the Mir before any more U.S. astronauts go on board for a long-term stay.
James Sensenbrenner asked NASA to comply voluntarily with legislation that would bar U.S. astronauts from going on board Mir for a long-term stay until the safety tests are passed.

The House recently passed a bill, the Civilian Space Authorisation, containing a rule that no U.S. astronaut be placed on board Mir for a long-term stay until the National Aeronatics and Space Administration certifies to Congress that the space station meets or exceeds U.S. safety standards. It is not yet law.
In Russia, officials put on brave face, saying that the situation on the station was under control. They said the crew has sufficient water and food supplies on board.
But Vladimir Solovyov, responsible for flight coordination at the Korolyov centre, conceded that an eighth of the Mir station was temporarily out of action because of the collision.
Lobachyov said a special commission comprising officials and experts had been set up to consider the situation and work our recommendation.

Interfax news agency quoted Russian officials as saying one more space walk by the cosmonauts may be needed to get the details of what had happened and estimate the damage. They did not say when the space walk would take place.
The launch of the next cargo craft, set for June 27, will probably be postponed, Lobachyov said.
He said the a commission would decide Spektr's fate and added that it might be undocked from the space station.
Lobachyov said the Progress was moving away from Mir and was expected to fall to Earth and sink into the Pacific Ocean on Friday.
Mir, the world's only space station, was launched in 1986 and has suffered a series of malfunctions in recent months, including a fire and a leakage of coolant.
The crew could be returned to Earth at short notice in a Russian Soyuz escape craft kept docked to Mir at all times. NASA said there was no immediate plan to evacuate the three men.
Mir is due to be replaced by an international station called Alpha in the next few years.
